## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Naomi saw that Ruth would be best cared for if she married, so she suggested Ruth ask Boaz to marry her. Guzik says the Hebrew word for "security/rest" is the same one used in 1:9, and that a home should be a place of rest and security. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Henry praises Naomi's care. She had settled on staying a widow herself but didn't hold the young Ruth to the same choice. He makes this a lesson: parents should seek this kind of "rest" for their children when the time is right. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm

**v. 2**
- Naomi's question "is he not our relative?" reminds Ruth that Boaz is a *goel* (kinsman-redeemer). Guzik lists the *goel*'s duties:
  - buying a relative out of slavery (Lev 25:48)
  - avenging a murdered relative (Num 35:19)
  - buying back family land
  - marrying a childless widow to carry on the family name

  In short, he protected the family's people, property and descendants. Guzik grants that Naomi could look like she was setting a trap for a reluctant man, but says the approach was seen as proper at the time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Ruth and Boaz had come to know each other over the harvest by seeing how each behaved around other people. Guzik contrasts this with modern "dating." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Boaz would be at the threshing floor all night, overseeing the winnowing and guarding his crop. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Naomi understood men well. She told Ruth to make herself attractive and to leave Boaz alone while he ate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Currid reads it differently. He notes that some commentators see the washing and perfume as seduction, but thinks they more likely showed that Ruth's time of mourning was over. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- Currid: Ruth waited until Boaz was alone so that her reputation would be protected if he said no. He calls it "not a case of scandalous entrapment." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: in that culture, uncovering the feet and lying down was not a sexual offer. It was what a servant did: lie at the master's feet, ready for orders. Ruth was claiming a real right, since Boaz was her *goel*, but Naomi had her come as a humble servant trusting his goodness rather than as a victim demanding her rights. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Guzik admits the plan could have gone badly. He quotes another commentator (unnamed in what I saw) who said it might have been "fatal to Ruth" if Boaz had not been so godly, and warned it "should in no sense be imitated." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Henry says the plan "looks suspicious." If anything was wrong with it, the blame lies with Naomi, who should have known Israel's laws and customs better than Ruth. He adds that the goodness of those days kept it from being wrong then, but that doesn't excuse anyone copying it now. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm
- Currid admits the command can look like a lure to sex, but argues the rest of the scene shows otherwise (see vv. 7–9). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/

**v. 5**
- Henry: Ruth was too good and too sensible to promise this if she had seen anything wrong in it. The young should accept the sound advice of their elders when they have no real objection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm

**v. 6–7**
- Guzik: Boaz slept by the grain because these were the unstable days of the judges, when thieves might steal a harvest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Currid: "his heart was merry" means he was content, not drunk or open to temptation. Translating "came softly" wrongly hints at a seductive approach. Ruth simply lifted the blanket, lay at his feet and covered herself, which pictured her wish to come under his protection as redeemer. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- JFB: Ruth lay crosswise at his feet. Eastern servants often slept that way in their master's room and were allowed to share part of his covering. Henry likewise says she lay across the foot of his bed, fully clothed, "not by his side," and stayed awake. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_003.cfm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm

**v. 8**
- Guzik pictures Boaz waking in the dark, sensing someone there but unable to see clearly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Currid: Boaz's question "who are you?" would make no sense if the two were in the middle of a sexual encounter. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/

**v. 9**
- Guzik: calling herself his "servant" shows humility. "Spread your garment over me" was the customary way for a widow to say "marry me." He cites Adam Clarke that Jewish bridegrooms in Clarke's day threw the edge of the tallit (prayer shawl) over the bride as a sign of protection. Calling Boaz *goel* shows the request was bold but not improper. It was the only way Elimelech's name could continue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Currid: the whole scene is a humble, virtuous request for Boaz to act as redeemer. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Boaz was apparently much older than Ruth and may have thought she would never want him. He could have claimed her by right as *goel* but wouldn't act unless she wanted it. Ruth, for her part, chose him for his character rather than his looks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/
- Henry: Ruth didn't seek, or even accept, the attention of young men. She was willing to marry an older man as God's law directed, for the good of her husband's family. He draws a lesson: young people should aim to please God and their parents more than their own eyes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Boaz's answer made Naomi's advice look wise. He was drawn by Ruth's character, and her courage and virtue make her a "Proverbs 31" kind of woman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-3/ (the Proverbs 31 point is from the Spanish edition: https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/rut-03/)
- Currid: the phrase "worthy woman" echoes how Boaz himself is described in 2:1. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- Henry: Ruth's virtue was well known even though she was poor. Her humility led to this honour, and good people who are poor will be honoured by God and others. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: there was a relative closer to Elimelech, and Boaz couldn't act unless that man gave up his right. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/rut-03/ ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/

**v. 13**
- Precept Austin quotes Arnold Fruchtenbaum: the Hebrew verb for "stay/remain" here is *lun*, not *shachav*. *Shachav* can carry a sexual meaning and *lun* does not, so the word choice removes any sexual suggestion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_313-18
- The same page says redemption in Ruth included levirate marriage (a relative marrying a dead man's widow) as well as buying back property. The aim was to keep the family name alive. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_313-18

**v. 14**
- Precept Austin: Ruth obeyed Boaz's command to stay, lying "at his feet, not by his side." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_313-18
- Currid: the scene shows restraint, and Boaz sent her off before dawn to protect her reputation. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- Henry: walking home in the dead of night wasn't safe, so she left at first light, before she could be recognised. Lesson: keep a good name as well as a good conscience, and avoid causing scandal as well as sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm
- Guzik reads the secrecy another way. They weren't hiding anything shameful; Boaz wanted to tell the nearer relative himself. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/rut-03/

**v. 15**
- Currid: the barley was Boaz's pledge to Ruth and Naomi that he would act that day. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/

**v. 16–17**
- Nothing specific in the pages I could see.

**v. 18**
- Henry: Ruth had done all that was right for her to do, and now had to wait calmly for the outcome. Lesson: leave our worries to God's providence and accept whatever comes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_003.cfm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ
I found no sources on this. The commentators above do disagree on some points (vv. 3, 4 and 14), but the pages don't present these as differences between traditions.

## 3. Other views
The only alternative readings I saw are ones Currid mentions in order to reject them:
- **v. 3:** some read Ruth's preparations as seduction.
- **v. 15:** some read the barley as payment for sex, like Judah's payment to Tamar in Genesis 38. Currid calls this view "unseemly."

He doesn't name who holds these views. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
